confidence=2.00 scores=[2, 2, 2] reasons=['The triad of unilateral facial pain (especially trigeminal distribution—cheek), painful sexual intercourse (suggesting vulvovaginal or pelvic involvement), and cutaneous blisters on the forearm strongly suggests a dermatomal herpes zoster (shingles) infection, possibly with multisegmental or atypical spread; however, the absence of key details—including lesion morphology (e.g., grouped vesicles vs. pustules), distribution (dermatomal vs. non-dermatomal), presence of prodromal symptoms, immunocompromised status, HIV/CD4 count, vaccination history, genital exam findings, and whether the cheek pain is truly dermatomal (V2/V3) or referred—prevents definitive diagnosis and rules out mimics like HSV, contact dermatitis, or autoimmune blistering disorders.  
DECISION: Somewhat Unconfident', 'The triad of unilateral facial pain (especially trigeminal distribution, triggered by eating), genital pain during intercourse, and cutaneous blisters on the forearm strongly suggests a reactivation of varicella-zoster virus (VZV) — i.e., herpes zoster — possibly with atypical or multidermatomal involvement (e.g., trigeminal (V1/V2/V3) and thoracic/brachial dermatomes), but critical details are missing: exact blister location/distribution (dermatomal vs. non-dermatomal), presence of prodromal symptoms, vesicle morphology (unilocular, grouped, umbilicated), sensory exam findings (hyperesthesia, allodynia), history of chickenpox or shingles, immunocompromised status, and absence or presence of ophthalmic involvement (which would elevate urgency); without dermatomal mapping and clinical exam, other conditions like herpes simplex virus (HSV) infection, contact dermatitis, or even autoimmune blistering diseases cannot be reliably excluded.  
DECISION: Somewhat Unconfident', 'The triad of unilateral facial pain (especially triggered by eating), genital pain during intercourse, and cutaneous blisters on the forearm strongly suggests a reactivation of varicella-zoster virus (VZV) — i.e., herpes zoster — possibly with atypical or multi-dermatomal involvement (e.g., trigeminal V1/V2 and thoracic/brachial dermatomes), but critical details are missing: exact blister distribution (dermatomal vs. scattered), presence of prodromal symptoms, fever, immunocompromised status, HIV testing, CSF or PCR confirmation, and whether the cheek pain is truly trigeminal neuralgia–like or associated with vesicles in the oral cavity or ear (to rule out Ramsay Hunt). Without dermatomal mapping, viral testing, or assessment for neurological deficits, other conditions (e.g., recurrent aphthous ulcers with referred pain, complex regional pain syndrome, or even early Behçet’s disease) cannot be reliably excluded.  
DECISION: Somewhat Unconfident']
